title: Electricity was never harnessed
premise: In 1831 induction experiments fail to give a steady current and no practical generator is ever found. The world keeps industrializing on coal, steam, town gas, hydraulic and compressed-air mains, and clockwork. Cities stay low, mechanical and pipe-bound, with diesel and steam doing what motors and wires do in ours.

chain.event: Michael Faraday's induction trials yield only faint, unsteady twitches and are set aside as a curiosity.
chain.consequence: Workshop investment and scientific interest shift to boilers, gas chemistry and thermodynamics, and no generator or electric motor enters industry.

chain.event: Trials of wire telegraphs without workable current are dropped, and administrations extend hilltop optical semaphore lines while cities lay iron pneumatic message tubes.
chain.consequence: Long-distance news travels by relayed visual signals and city messages travel as paper capsules in air pipes, keeping offices clustered near tube stations and signal towers.

chain.event: The incandescent gas mantle is perfected for street and interior lamps.
chain.consequence: Municipal gasworks expand coal-gas mains to whole districts, and bright gas lighting keeps shops, workshops and streets active after dark without any wiring.

chain.event: Spark-ignition petrol engines prove unreliable without an electric spark, while compression-ignition diesel engines and improved steam traction engines succeed.
chain.consequence: Road haulage and farm work standardize on heavy diesel lorries with air starters and on coal-fired steam tractors, with fuel yards, water towers and repair forges along every main road.

chain.event: Compressed-air mains and hydraulic power mains are copied in large ports and manufacturing towns.
chain.consequence: Central pumping stations send high-pressure air and water through street pipes to run lifts, machine tools and shop hoists, keeping factories small, low and close to the mains.

chain.event: Mechanical information systems reach maturity with high-speed punched-card tabulators, clockwork calculators and long-distance copy by pneumatic post and optical relay.
chain.consequence: Banks, railways and administrations occupy broad low buildings filled with clerks and steel calculating machines, circulating printed bulletins and timetables instead of instant electronic signals.

eras.caption: 1926 · Gas lamps and steam carts
eras.visualPrompt: Transform this scene to 1926 in a world where electricity was never harnessed. Show low blocks in the region's own building tradition with chimneys and gas lamps, horse carts and a steam traction engine filling the street.
eras.visualPromptIndoor: Interior of an office lit by wall gas mantles, with wooden desks, brass clockwork calculators and a pneumatic capsule station.

differences: Four- to six-storey masonry blocks instead of taller steel towers (because hydraulic and steam lifts and daylight limit practical height)
Horse teams, bicycles and hissing steam traction engines on the street instead of petrol cars and electric trams (because spark ignition and electric motors never arrived)
Tall cast-iron gas lamps and wall-mounted gas pipes instead of electric streetlights (because coal-gas mains with incandescent mantles light streets and shopfronts)
Rooftop semaphore posts and street pneumatic tube stations instead of telephone wires and radio masts (because messages travel as paper capsules and visual signals)
Chimneys, coal yards and low boiler houses on every block instead of hidden substations (because heat and workshop power come from local coal and steam mains)

Round gas lanterns and district steam pipes on facades instead of LED streetlights and buried electric cables (because coal-gas and piped heat serve every street)
Painted shop boards and gas-lit display windows instead of glowing screens and billboards (because steam printing presses and gaslight carry news and advertising)
Rooftop greenhouses, coal bunkers and water tanks instead of air-conditioning units and solar panels (because fuel storage and food growing sit on roofs above workshops)

Rows of gas lanterns and insulated heat mains on brackets instead of electric lighting columns and cable ducts (because town gas and central boilers heat and light whole streets)
Painted enamel timetables and printed bulletin kiosks instead of digital displays (because punched-card presses and optical relays circulate information on paper)

differences: Low tended masonry quarters draped in gardens instead of tall glass districts (because hydraulic care and daylight keep buildings low while planting cools rooms)
Tree-lined steam rail paths and cycle ways instead of multi-lane motor roads (because slow steam and muscle power move people between garden districts)
Mossed gas lanterns and vine-covered heat mains instead of electric lighting grids (because town gas and piped hot water still heat and light tended streets)
Canal basins, orchards and timber fuel yards between blocks instead of parking structures (because barges, horses and steam haulers bring coal, timber and food)
